title: Hosanna in the temple (Matthew 21:1–17)
hookLine: children shout hosanna in the temple; the leaders object; he quotes a psalm
carry: out of the mouths of babes
tomorrow: two sons: one says yes, one says no. which one did the father's will?
last: THAT OUR EYES MAY BE OPENED.

lines: A SHOUT IN THE QUIET PART.
cards: A toddler shouts the last line of a song a beat too late, in the quiet part, and heads turn. Some people smile. Some wince.
Matthew has a scene like that. Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a donkey, and the crowds cry, "Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest."
In the temple he overturns the moneychangers' tables, and the blind and the lame come to him there, and he heals them.
And then the children pick up the crowd's words and start shouting them, right in the temple: Hosanna to the son of David.

teach.b: The chief priests and scribes are sore displeased. "Hearest thou what these say?" And here is the answer to yesterday's question.

teach.h: OUT OF THE MOUTH OF BABES.
teach.b: Jesus quotes their own scripture back: "Yea; have ye never read, Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings thou hast perfected praise?" That line is from Psalm eight. The leaders heard noise.
He heard praise. Now a question Christians still argue over, kindly: where do children belong in worship? Some churches keep children in the whole service.
Their case: this very scene. The children were in the temple, loud, and he defended them.

Faith is learned by being in the room, wiggles and all, and a church that sends its kids out may be telling them the real thing is for adults. Other churches hold children's worship for part of the service.
Their case is strong too: kids praise more fully with songs and words made for them, at their pace, and parents get a few quiet minutes to listen.

teach.h: OUT OF THE MOUTHS OF BABES.
teach.b: Jesus' line, they'd say, is about praise, not about the seating chart. Hear what both sides already agree on. Neither calls a child's praise noise.
The argument is about how best to make room for it.

how: On Palm Sunday some churches hand out palms and some have children lead the procession; churches differ on whether children stay for the whole service or have their own worship for part of it.

games.q: what does “hosanna in the temple” mean?
o: a festival song sung by the temple priests
children's praise Jesus defended in the temple
a royal decree read out at the city gate

s: Jesus told the children to quiet down in the temple
he defended them with Psalm 8: out of the mouth of babes and sucklings thou hast perfected praise.
the line 'out of the mouth of babes' is Jesus quoting a psalm

the only thing Jesus did in the temple that day was overturn tables

games.q: your church is debating moving kids to their own worship time. you want them to stay in the main service. what's the other side's best case?
o: kids may praise more fully with songs and words made for them.
children's praise doesn't really count until they understand it.
worship has to be silent to count as real worship.
games.why: the strongest case for children's worship is about making room for their praise, not shushing it. both sides agree with Jesus: a child's praise is not noise.

practice: For the sit, listen for the smallest live sound you can hear: a kid outside, a bird, a neighbor's radio, the hum of the building.
Don't judge it as noise or music; let it be part of the room, the way the children's shouting was part of the temple.

wordCard.voice: Hosanna in the temple. The children's shout that the leaders wanted stopped, and Jesus called praise.

orig.note: Greek: hosanna, as Matthew writes the crowd's cry in 21:9 and the children's in 21:15.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: out of the mouths of babes, praise made perfect. That's the day.
